Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would create a system for facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism to earn tradable credits for staying below their emissions baselines.

It amends the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Act 2007 and the Australian National Registry of Emissions Units Act 2011 to set up how Safeguard Mechanism Credits are issued, bought, and recorded.
The government says the changes are part of a plan to meet Australia's legislated emissions targets, including net zero by 2050 and a 43% cut by 2030.
Enable facilities below their baselines to generate tradable Safeguard Mechanism Credits.
Phase out eligible offsets projects at Safeguard-covered facilities.
Amend the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative) Act 2011 to start implementing the government's response to an independent review of Australian Carbon Credit Units.
Facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism, and businesses that operate them.

The majority voted in favour of an amendment to the usual second reading motion, which is "*That this bill be now read a second time.*" To [read a bill for a second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/) is to agree with its main idea. This amendment does not make any changes to the bill itself but still has political significance because it represents the will of the Senate. It was introduced by Victorian Senator [Lidia Thorpe](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/lidia_thorpe) (Independent). ### Amendment text > *At the end of the motion, add “, but the Senate calls on the Government to:* > > *(a) in line with its commitment to implementing recommendation 9.8 of the final report of the [Pepper Scientific Inquiry into Hydraulic Fracturing in the Northern Territory](https://territorygas.nt.gov.au/sustainability-and-responsibility/the-scientific-inquiry-into-hydraulic-fracturing), ensure the gas industry in the Northern Territory’s Beetaloo Basin is required to offset all Scope 2 and 3 emissions by referring this matter to the Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council, and work with the Northern Territory Government to achieve this;* > > *(b) support First Nations communities in carbon sequestration projects on Country, including but not limited to savanna burning, and on Sea Country, including but not limited to kelp farming; and* > > *(c) support First Nations-led verification assessment of environmental, social and cultural values of carbon farming and sequestration projects and invest in training for these purposes in First Nations communities, including but not limited to communities in regional and remote areas and on missions and reserves”.*

The coalition opposed the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022, arguing it imposes a hidden carbon tax of $75 per tonne that will raise costs for consumers and force businesses to close, while Labor and Greens speakers supported the bill as necessary to meet Australia's 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 and net zero by 2050.

The speech argued that the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 is essential for meeting Australia’s climate targets of 43% emissions reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050, citing support from business and industry groups such as ACCI, BP, the Clean Energy Council, and Rio Tinto. It also criticised the Coalition for opposing the policy, which builds on their own previous safeguard mechanism, and for failing to take climate action seriously.

The Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill would cause de-industrialisation and loss of productive agricultural land, as industrial giants buy land for carbon credits, and the required 4.9% annual emissions reduction would make many industries unviable, leading to higher costs and offshoring of manufacturing.

The speaker announced a procedural resolution to extend debate on the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 tonight from 8 to 10 pm after the normal adjournment debate, avoiding cuts to speaking times or late sittings, with no vote tonight and a review tomorrow.

The speaker argued for the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022, claiming it would ensure net aggregate safeguard baselines decline and create tradable credits to incentivise emissions reductions. Specific figures mentioned include a 43 per cent emissions reduction target by 2030 on 2005 levels and $1.9 billion in the Powering the Regions Fund to assist safeguard facilities.

Senator Duniam moved a motion noting the minister’s failure to comply with an order for documents on Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs), rejecting the minister’s claim of public interest immunity, and postponing the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 until the documents and modelling are tabled. He stated the documents are sensitive and cabinet-in-confidence and cannot be released.

The Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 was opposed on the grounds that it would disadvantage domestic cement and lime manufacturers by imposing costs not applied to imports, risking closure of local plants and increased reliance on higher-emission overseas production, while the industry has already reduced emissions by 25% since 1990 and is committed to further decarbonisation once viable technologies become available.

The speaker argued they could not support the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 in its current form due to unresolved concerns, including the unlimited use of offsets and reliance on Australian carbon credit units, but would not vote against it. They noted the bill would affect 215 large emitters, including Rio Tinto's Bell Bay smelter in their electorate, and called for greater collaboration and amendments in the Senate.

The debate on the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 centred on whether it delivers genuine emissions cuts or functions as a new tax. Supporters argued it would save 205 million tonnes of emissions by 2030 and help achieve a 43% cut, while coalition opponents labelled it a carbon tax of $75–$100 a tonne that would hurt households and industry; the Greens criticised it for allowing new coal and gas projects and rising pollution through offsets.

The community Independent movement has reinvigorated democracy, with Wakehurst set to have Independent representation across all three levels of government for the first time and Pittwater too close to call, as once-safe seats shift because voters want representatives who listen and work across party lines. Community Independent MPs have helped pass the National Anti-Corruption Commission Bill 2022, the Climate Change Bill 2022 target, and the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2023.

The Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2023 passed the House and was expected to pass the Senate, with the minister arguing the reforms strengthen the economy by linking decarbonisation to economic success. The reforms were welcomed by the Business Council (as 'tough but achievable'), Climate Council, Australian Conservation Foundation, Australian Industry Group, and Investor Group on Climate Change, while the opposition was criticised for disagreeing with business.

The Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022 passed the House, delivering 205 million tonnes of emissions reductions by 2030 and requiring Australia's highest emitters to meet a proportional share of the 43 per cent national target. The speaker urged the Senate to pass the bill before 1 July 2023 to avoid missing the 2030 target.

The MP argued that the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2022, backed by Labor and the Greens, will block 116 coal, oil and gas projects—including Woodside’s Scarborough and Shell’s Crux fields—risking jobs for 60,000 FIFO workers in Western Australia and causing deindustrialisation, while household electricity prices are set to rise 56% over two years.

Senator Duniam moved to suspend standing orders to allow scrutiny of government amendments to the Safeguard Mechanism Bill, arguing the amendments were a secret deal with the Greens that would raise power prices, offshore emissions, and cost jobs, and that the government had broken its repeated promise to cut power bills by $275.

The minister argued that the Safeguard Mechanism reforms will reduce net and gross emissions from covered facilities, with a hard cap of 1,233 million tonnes to 2030 and a single-year target of 100 megatons. The bill includes a $75 per tonne cost containment measure, a $275 per tonne penalty, and adjusted baseline decline rates of 1–2% for trade-exposed industries, while 371 human-induced regeneration projects will be subject to independent audits under the Chubb review.
The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to immediately report and consider a Senate message on the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2023; the motion was agreed to.

The speaker moved to agree to amendments to the Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2023, arguing they reflect the government's election mandate and will limit coal and gas pollution for the first time in law. Opposition speakers claimed the bill amounts to a carbon tax that will raise prices, reduce investment, and harm manufacturing, while the Greens said the amendments impose a hard cap on pollution that will block about half of 116 proposed new coal and gas projects.

Senator Duniam argued the safeguard mechanism bill would increase costs, destroy jobs, and offshore emissions, criticising the Labor-Greens deal and lack of consultation on specific facilities like V/Line and rail freight. Senator McAllister defended the bill as necessary for climate action, citing extensive industry consultation and support from groups like the Minerals Council and BP, but declined to guarantee no job losses or provide facility-level cost modelling.

The Coalition senator argued the Safeguard Mechanism bill and the Labor-Greens deal would increase costs for households and businesses, citing potential rate rises for Perth's Red Hill Waste Management Facility, higher fuel prices from Ampol's Lytton refinery, and increased V/Line train fares, while criticising the government for not consulting the 215 covered facilities on specific impacts or ruling out job losses.

The Safeguard Mechanism (Crediting) Amendment Bill 2023 passed the Senate, with Minister Wong arguing the reforms provide overdue policy certainty for climate action and the economy, while criticising the Coalition for lacking a plan to deliver net zero by 2050.
